questions.question: What happens by default when you bind untrusted, attacker-controlled HTML to `[innerHTML]` in Angular?
options: The HTML executes exactly as written, including any script-like handlers
Angular's built-in sanitizer strips dangerous content before it reaches the DOM
Angular throws a compile-time error and refuses to build
The binding silently does nothing at all
questions.explanation: Angular automatically sanitizes values passed into security-sensitive bindings like innerHTML, removing dangerous constructs like inline event handlers.

questions.question: What does calling `sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(...)` actually do?
options: It sanitizes the HTML more strictly than the default
It tells Angular to skip sanitization entirely for that value, trusting the developer that it's safe
It encrypts the HTML before rendering
It has no real effect; it's purely for documentation
questions.explanation: The bypassSecurityTrust* methods are an explicit opt-out of Angular's sanitization — they should never be used on raw, unreviewed user input.

questions.question: Why is calling `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` on raw user-submitted content dangerous?
options: It has a performance cost but no security impact
It disables the protection Angular normally provides against XSS, potentially allowing a user-submitted script-like payload to execute
It only affects styling, not security
It's dangerous only in development mode, not production
questions.explanation: Bypassing sanitization on attacker-controlled input re-opens the exact XSS vector that automatic sanitization exists to close.

questions.question: Why is a token-based auth setup (Authorization header via an interceptor) generally less vulnerable to CSRF than cookie-based auth?
options: Tokens can't be stolen under any circumstances
Browsers don't automatically attach custom headers like Authorization to cross-site requests the way they automatically attach cookies
CSRF only affects GET requests, and tokens are only used for POST
There is no actual difference in CSRF exposure
questions.explanation: CSRF relies on the browser automatically including credentials (cookies) on cross-site requests; a bearer token in a header must be explicitly attached by your own JS, which a malicious site cannot do on your behalf.
